name: Dimorphism theory

card.summary: The idea that more sex-typical (masculine or feminine) facial features raise attractiveness; research on it is real but mixed.
card.note: Studies disagree on whether masculine male faces are rated as more attractive, and preferences vary by culture and context.

quick.overview:
Dimorphism theory is the looksmaxxing framing that faces differ between the sexes in measurable ways, and that more strongly sex-typical features (a pronounced jaw and brow in men, softer and more youthful features in women) are more attractive. Communities use it to explain why certain faces are rated highly.

Research on facial sexual dimorphism does exist, but its findings on attractiveness are mixed and depend on the population, culture, and what other traits are controlled for.
quick.mechanism: Proponents point to hormones, especially testosterone during puberty, shaping facial bone and soft tissue, and argue that observers read these features as signals of health or genetic quality. Researchers have proposed similar signalling hypotheses, while noting that the supporting evidence is inconsistent.
quick.risks: The theory itself is a descriptive framework with no direct risk. Applications that community members discuss, such as hormone use or surgery to change facial structure, carry their own medical risks that are covered in separate entries.

lead: Dimorphism theory is the looksmaxxing framework that treats how masculine or feminine a face and body look as a main driver of attractiveness. Members use it as a checklist for improvement: a strong jaw, defined brow and broad frame for men, and softer, more youthful features for women, with grooming, body composition, hair, facial hair and sometimes procedures chosen to push features toward the sex-typical end.[3][4] The practical payoff people describe is concrete: leanness that reveals the jaw and cheekbones, facial hair and brow styling, shoulder and frame training, and a vocabulary for deciding what to work on.

The idea overlaps with an academic literature on facial sexual dimorphism. A widely cited review of the evolutionary psychology of facial beauty argued that averageness, symmetry and sexual dimorphism are good candidates for biologically based standards of attractiveness, with meta-analyses indicating that all three are attractive in male and female faces across cultures.[5] A 2011 review likewise lists sexually dimorphic shape among the features that affect attractiveness judgments, alongside symmetry, averageness and skin colour, and describes preferences as flexible, shaped by hormones, fertility, experience and social learning.[15] Other work reports that preferences for masculine male faces vary with menstrual-cycle phase, hormonal contraception, relationship context and country.[2][18]

Because the term is a community framework rather than a single formal theory, forum discussion ranges from simple observations about height and jaw width to measurement schemes, such as a lower-face-to-skull-height ratio, to composite ratings that combine golden-ratio scores with dimorphism scores, and to questions about whether testosterone changes the face.[4][7][8][21] Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article lists features the culture prizes, including a defined jawline, hollow cheeks and so-called hunter eyes, and describes the wider scene, which uses terms such as softmaxxing and hardmaxxing for non-invasive versus substance and surgery based approaches.[11]

chain: Identify which features read as masculine or feminine
Improve those features through grooming, leanness, training or procedures
Face and body read as more sex-typical
angle.text: Members use dimorphism as a lens for choosing what to work on: leaner faces that show the jaw and cheekbones, brow and facial-hair styling for men, and softer, youthful features for women. Proponents say moving features toward the sex-typical end raises how attractive a face is rated.

infobox: More sex-typical facial features are rated as more attractive
Jaw width, brow ridge, cheekbones, lower-face height, facial hair, skin tone
Males about 13 cm taller than females[6]
About 10 to 20 times higher in males[6]
Mixed findings across studies and cultures

paras: In forum discussion the term describes how masculine or feminine a face appears, with features such as jaw width, brow ridge, cheekbone prominence and facial hair on one side and softer, more youthful proportions on the other. Members use it to explain ratings and to decide which features to improve.[1]

Outside the community the subject is studied as sexual dimorphism and facial masculinity or femininity. In humans, males on average are taller and heavier than females and have denser bones, with testosterone levels roughly ten to twenty times higher in adult males.[1] Hair distribution, skin thickness and colour, and body proportions also differ on average.[1]

Wikipedia's overview of human physiological dimorphism reports that males average about 13 cm taller than females, with roughly a quarter of the difference attributed to the Y chromosome and another quarter to testicular androgens. Females have larger hips relative to the waist and a higher percentage of body fat, guided by estrogen at puberty, and male bone mineral density is about 34 percent higher in raw terms (about 8 percent higher at the hip after adjusting for height and weight).[6] Adult male testosterone is roughly 300 to 1,000 ng/dL against 15 to 70 ng/dL in adult females, and testosterone rises about tenfold at male puberty.[6] The article does not itself cover jaw or brow dimorphism, which is the area community discussion focuses on.[6]

Wikipedia's article on neoteny in humans lists retained-youthful facial traits such as reduced brow ridges, larger eyes, a small nose and a shorter lower face, and reports a cross-cultural study in which more neotenised female faces were rated most attractive by men.[12] Looksmaxxing posters often use neoteny and dimorphism as paired ideas: robust, large-boned features on one side and youthful features on the other, with disagreement in forum threads about which traits belong in which camp.[3][12]

The academic study of facial dimorphism and attractiveness took off in the 1990s, when researchers began using computer-averaged and morphed faces to test preferences directly. A 1998 Nature study by Perrett and colleagues had participants pick the most attractive faces from continua that exaggerated or reduced the difference between average female and male face shapes, in UK and Japanese populations.[13] Reviews in the following decades, including Rhodes in 2006 and Little and colleagues in 2011, collected the findings under evolutionary and mate-choice frameworks.[5][15]

In looksmaxxing, the vocabulary developed on forums. Wikipedia reports that the term looksmaxxing was coined on incel message boards in the 2010s, where PSL-style rating scales and vocabulary were shaped by sites such as PUAHate, Sluthate and Lookism.net, all now defunct, and that the practice spread to TikTok in the early 2020s, initially in a self-improvement framing.[11] Dimorphism is one of several dimensions forum members use when rating faces, together with ratios, symmetry and side profile, and the topic appears in threads that argue looks are subjective because of dimorphism and in threads that share measurement templates.[3][4][21]

A looksmax.org thread on the topic argues that dimorphism underlies much of why looks seem subjective, pointing to height pairing, skin tone and youthfulness as traits that differ by sex and shape partner preferences; replies in the same thread dispute which traits count as masculine, feminine or simply robust or neotenous.[3]

Another thread reposts a measurement attributed to a facial-analysis site: the distance from chin to eyeline divided by chin to top of skull, described as a way to quantify lower-face height, with a taller lower third described as a masculine trait and a stated male range of about 50 to 53 percent.[4] Posters in that thread asked how the ranges are defined, illustrating that these metrics are community conventions.[4]
A further forum thread asks how far craniofacial development, and facial dimorphism in particular, can still change at the end of the teen years.[8]

sections.h: Facial features and the research on them
paras: The Wikipedia article on facial attractiveness reports that heterosexual women tend on average to prefer masculine facial dimorphism, that angular male jaws are favoured in Western countries while rounder, softer female jaws are preferred, and that men with less submental fat were seen as having better jawlines.[2] The same article reports that light facial hair was rated most attractive on male faces, and that beard growth depends on testosterone.[2] Wikipedia's article on sexual selection in humans adds that facial hair is a status signal linked to perceived dominance, and that a 2019 study found facial hair makes the jaw look more prominent and anger displays easier to read.[9]

On the female side, the facial-attractiveness article reports a 2008 Italian study of 324 adolescents in which 93 attractive individuals, drawn from a casting agency, had more neotenous (youthful) features, with the older attractive boys also showing some sexual dimorphism. A 1995 study by Cunningham found judges preferred a mix of youthful and sexually mature features, with mature features at the face's periphery and youthful features at its centre.[2] It also reports that more feminine female faces tend to be rated as more attractive, and that East Asian women's faces were rated as more prototypically feminine in several follow-up studies.[2]

A 2006 Annual Review of Psychology paper by Rhodes concluded from meta-analyses that sexual dimorphism is attractive in both sexes across cultures while discussing whether such preferences are adaptations or by-products of how brains process faces.[5] Individual studies are less uniform. Perrett and colleagues reported in 1998 that participants preferred feminised shapes over average and masculinised male faces, and that masculinisation raised perceived dominance and traits such as coldness or dishonesty; the authors concluded that selection pressure limits dimorphism and favours youthful features.[13] A 2010 PLoS ONE study by Scott and colleagues measured masculinity with geometric morphometrics and reported no relationship between morphological masculinity and rated attractiveness in men, while skin colour did predict attractiveness.[14]

Research on how observers respond to facial masculinity is mixed. One strand reports that women in the high-estrogen follicular phase were more likely to choose masculine faces than women who were menstruating or using hormonal contraception, interpreted under the so-called sexy son hypothesis.[2] Another reports that women who rate themselves as more attractive tend to prefer more masculine faces.[2]

Other work cited in the same review found no association between male facial masculinity and attractiveness among female judges, even while more feminine female faces were rated as more attractive, and one study argued that once perceived health is removed, masculinity makes little difference to male attractiveness.[2] A survey of heterosexual men in 28 countries found a preference for feminised female faces, stronger where national health indices were higher.[2]

The Annual Review of Psychology paper by Rhodes takes a broader view, concluding from meta-analyses that sexual dimorphism is attractive in both sexes across cultures, and discussing whether such preferences are adaptations for mate choice or by-products of how brains process faces.[5]

Cultural and contextual variation is a recurring theme. The facial-attractiveness article reports a study of 4,794 women in their early twenties that found national differences in masculinity preference, and a survey by Marcinkowska and colleagues of heterosexual men in 28 countries in which feminised female faces were preferred, with stronger preferences in countries with higher National Health Index scores; Japan showed the strongest femininity preference and Nepal the weakest.[2] A study cited in the sexual-selection article found British women preferred male faces with low cortisol while Latvian women did not discriminate by cortisol level, which the authors interpreted as reflecting societal-level ecological factors.[9]

Wikipedia also reports that masculinity has been proposed as an indicator of health or status but that its link to health has been questioned, that in men facial masculinity correlates with symmetry, and that one genetic study found the same genes that produce masculine male faces produce feminine-leaning traits in sisters.[2] The sexual-selection article reports that women in the fertile phase of their cycle showed greater preference for masculine voices, body size and face shape in one study, and that men's attraction to feminine faces was highest when their own testosterone was highest.[9]

A 2003 study in Proceedings of the Royal Society B asked whether dimorphism signals health: masculine traits in adolescent male faces correlated modestly with actual health but were not rated as attractive, while feminine female faces were rated as healthy and attractive without a correlation with health.[17] A 2009 study of men found that those with more masculine faces showed higher circulating testosterone after winning a competitive task, although baseline testosterone was not related to facial masculinity.[17] In a 2002 study, women's preference for masculinity in male faces depended on partnership status and the temporal context of a relationship.[18]

Newer studies continue to report context effects. Papers from 2025 report that exposure to violence was associated with a stronger preference for masculinised faces in Senegal, that women's sociosexuality and self-rated mate value did not significantly predict their preferences for masculine male face shape, and that handgrip strength was not reliably related to facial dimorphism in Czech and Cameroonian samples.[19]

T Nation hosts a forum thread titled around whether testosterone replacement builds more masculine facial features, quoting an article in which a writer reports noticing more pronounced facial changes alongside muscle gain after starting treatment.[7] Hormone use carries its own medical considerations and is covered in separate entries.

Controlled research on hormones and social perception has examined behaviour more than faces. A randomized, double-blind study of 139 Chinese men found that a single dose of testosterone gel reduced their sensitivity to vocal cues of other men's dominance compared with placebo.[10] Wikipedia reports that exogenous testosterone reduced men's preference for feminine female faces in long-term relationship contexts in one study.[9] Studies of how testosterone reshapes the adult face are lacking, which is why forum users compare personal photos in threads like the T Nation one above.[7]

Within the community, dimorphism functions as a vocabulary for goals. Softmaxxing practices such as skincare, grooming, fitness and posture are described in Wikipedia's account as non-invasive routes, and hardmaxxing as substances and surgery aimed at a more masculine appearance; the same article notes that coverage by outlets including Vice, The New York Times, The Guardian and the BBC between 2018 and 2026 has examined the scene, and that critics such as Rosdahl in The Conversation have raised concerns about radicalisation and body image.[11] Members who share facial measurements often add that images can be altered by filters, makeup, angle and facial bloating, as one looksmax.org composite-ranking thread notes.[21]
Related entries in this wiki cover the procedures and compounds that threads connect to dimorphism, such as jaw surgery, facial hair, testosterone therapy and leanness through body-fat reduction.

No studies found on dimorphism theory as a looksmaxxing framework or on interventions designed on its basis. Related laboratory and survey research on facial masculinity, femininity and perceived attractiveness exists and is summarised above.[2][5]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org dimorphism is treated as a central axis for judging faces and for choosing improvements, and is discussed alongside ratios and symmetry.[3][4]

claims.claim: Dimorphism is the main reason looks differ in how they are rated
claims.believers: Forum members argue that men and women each prefer partners who are more sex-typical than themselves, citing height, skin tone and youthfulness.[3]
claims.experts: Reviews report that sexual dimorphism is attractive in both sexes in meta-analyses, while individual studies of masculine male faces disagree and vary by context.[5][2]

claims.claim: A taller lower third of the face is a masculine trait that raises dimorphism
claims.believers: Posters share a chin-to-eyeline over chin-to-vertex ratio and cite an ideal male band of about 50 to 53 percent.[4]
claims.experts: No published study was found validating that specific ratio as a predictor of rated attractiveness.

claims.claim: Higher testosterone builds a more masculine face
claims.believers: A T Nation thread quotes a writer who says men on testosterone therapy notice changes above the neck as well as in muscle.[7]
claims.experts: Reviews note that testosterone drives pubertal growth of male bone and soft tissue, and that effects in adults are less well documented.[1]

claims.claim: Women prefer masculine faces, so a masculine jaw and brow raise attractiveness
claims.believers: Forum members treat masculine dimorphism as a baseline for male attractiveness and pursue jaw, brow and leanness changes accordingly.[3][4]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that heterosexual women tend on average to prefer masculine dimorphism, but that preference shifts with cycle phase, contraception use, self-rated attractiveness, relationship context and country, and that one study found male facial masculinity did not predict attractiveness for female judges.[2]

claims.claim: Feminine, youthful features are the key to female attractiveness across cultures
claims.believers: Posters describe softer, neotenous features, skin tone and youthfulness as the female counterpart to male masculinity.[3]
claims.experts: A survey of men in 28 countries found a general preference for feminised faces, strongest in countries with better national health indices, and a cross-cultural study reported that more neotenised female faces were preferred regardless of age.[2]

claims.claim: Masculinised male faces are more attractive to women.
claims.believers: Members treat a pronounced jaw and brow as a baseline for male attractiveness and work on leanness, facial hair and frame to show them.[3][4]
claims.experts: Perrett and colleagues found participants preferred feminised male shapes over masculinised ones in 1998, while Scott and colleagues found no link between measured masculinity and rated attractiveness in 2010; other reports describe context effects.[13][14][18]

claims.claim: Dimorphism signals health or genetic quality.
claims.believers: Posters argue masculine and feminine traits advertise hormonal health, echoing signalling hypotheses.[3]
claims.experts: A 2003 study found masculinity in adolescent male faces modestly correlated with health but was not rated attractive, and femininity in female faces did not correlate with health although it was rated attractive.[17]

claims.believers: Forum users link a masculine face to high testosterone and ask whether therapy adds facial change.[7][8]
claims.experts: A 2009 study reported that more masculine-faced men had higher circulating testosterone after winning a competition, with no link to baseline levels.[17]

claims.claim: A neotenous, youthful face is the female ideal across cultures.
claims.believers: Posters describe youthfulness and softness as the female counterpart to masculinity.[3]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports a cross-cultural study in which more neotenised female faces were rated most attractive by men.[12]
